newsitem.title: JAPAN: Opposition attacks Japan PM for economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Opposition attacks Japan PM for economic policy.

text.p: Japan's opposition parties on Wednesday blamed Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's 1997 budget plan for falling financial markets and attacked his handling of the country's worst-ever oil slick.

Kicking off debate in a 1997 parliament session in which opposition disunity could be Hashimoto's greatest strength, Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) and the Democratic Party -- the two largest opposition groups -- seized on recent dire headlines to attack the prime minister.
"Plunges in stock prices since the New Year sound a grave alarm bell for the Hashimoto administration," Shinshinto President Ichiro Ozawa told parliament's lower house.
"The direct cause of (the plunges of the yen, stock and bond prices) is the government's budget for 1997," he said.
Ozawa called the 77.39 trillion yen ($655 billion) spending scheme heavy with pork-barrel politics and likely to increase government red ink.
Democratic Party leader Naoto Kan, a key campaigner for slimmer government and reduced spending, also said market turmoil reflected "despair at the budget plan".
However, the opposition's attacks may have come one day too late to make a maximum impact.

Even as the two leaders spoke, the stock market was staging a rally, rising more than four percent after dramatic falls in recent sessions because of worries that not enough was being done to revive the economy.

Ozawa, who advocates a more robust Japanese stance on defence and crisis management, blasted as "deplorably tardy" the government reaction to an oil spill from a sunken Russian tanker that has fouled a 900-km (550 mile) strip of Japan's coast.
Hashimoto on Tuesday had admitted his government had "misjudged" the seriousness of the maritime disaster.
Japan's opposition parties fared poorly in general elections last October for the 500-seat Lower House of parliament and have proliferated in number as a result of splits and defections.

The electorate also refused to give Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party a majority, forcing it to form a loose alliance with two small parties that were full coalition partners with the LDP from 1994-96.
The LDP at present has 240 seats, Shinshinto 142 and the Democrats 52.

A poll published by the mass circulation Yomiuri Shimbun daily newspaper on Wednesday showed the popularity of Hashimoto's cabinet had slipped nearly five percentage points to 51.8 percent in January compared to the previous month.
The decline in support was partly attributed to government failure to outline clear-cut fiscal reconstruction measures, the newspaper said.
